# Measurements

## What is a spinorama set of graphs?

A Spinorama is a standardized set of loudspeaker responses intended to make
directivity and tonal behavior easier to compare. The method is defined by the
US [CTA](https://cta.tech); see the [standard method of measurement](https://shop.cta.tech/products/standard-method-of-measurement-for-in-home-loudspeakers)
for the formal definitions.

Here is an example:
![Genelec 8341A](https://www.spinorama.org/docs/images/Genelec-8341A-CEA2034.png)

The spinorama gives you a few graphs:

- *On Axis:* the response directly in front of the speaker. A smooth response
  is generally easier to equalize.
- *Listening Window:* an average of responses near the on-axis direction. It
  represents small changes in listening position better than a single trace.
- *Early Reflections:* an estimate of the first reflected energy in a typical
  room. It is usually smoother and slopes downward with frequency.
- *Sound Power:* an average over the full measurement sphere. Its slope is
  often greater than that of Early Reflections for conventional speakers.
- *ERDI and SPDI:* the differences between the Early Reflection curve and the
  Listening Window (or Sound Power and Listening Window). Smooth, predictable
  directivity is generally easier to equalize. Equalization cannot repair
  large directivity errors because it cannot make off-axis sound follow the
  on-axis correction.

The speaker above is *very* good. You can compare with another one:

![Tannoy XT6](https://www.spinorama.org/docs/images/Tannoy-Revolution-XT6-CEA2034.png)

which has larger tonal deviations. A 3 dB change is a substantial acoustic
change, but it does not mean that perceived loudness doubles or halves. If the
on-axis response rises toward the treble, the speaker may sound brighter in a
typical listening setup.

![Tannoy XT6](https://www.spinorama.org/docs/images/Tannoy-Revolution-XT6-ON.png)

# How to select a speaker

Speaker choice depends on the room, listening distance, budget, and priorities.
The measurements are evidence to combine with those practical constraints,
not a replacement for listening.

## Criteria

Useful criteria include:

- *Price*: Price is not a reliable proxy for measured performance. Consider
  value, warranty, and local availability.
- *Design*: Choose the form factor, directivity, and features that fit the
  room and your preferences.
- *Build quality*: Check independent reviews, warranty terms, and repair
  support rather than inferring them from measurements.
- *Support quality*: Consider replacement parts, service availability, and the
  length and coverage of the warranty.
- *Tonality*: Preference scores combine several response characteristics. They
  are useful for comparisons, but they do not measure every aspect of sound
  quality.
- *Maximum output*: Decide how loud you need to listen and at what distance.
  SPL capability depends on room size, listening distance, bass content, and
  distortion limits.

- *Bass extension*: Small speakers generally need a subwoofer for deep bass at
  high levels. DSP can extend bass from a small cabinet, but maximum output
  and distortion still matter. Consider the kind of content you listen to and
  the level you need.

  You can choose floorstanders or bookshelves with subwoofers. Integration is
  not always easy, but it is practical with careful placement and calibration.

## How good is your room?

- Is the room dedicated to music?
- Is the room symmetrical?
- Does it have some absorption?
- Have you added panels to control reflections?
- Do you have multiple subwoofers to control bass linearity?
- Have you measured the speakers in the room?
- Are you using room-correction software?

If the room is untreated or the listening position is unknown, room acoustics
and placement may matter more than small score differences. A speaker with
smooth directivity is usually easier to integrate and equalize, but no
spinorama predicts every room.

## How to interpret the numbers on the landing page?

Each speaker measurement shows up in a box similar to:

![Example for one speaker on the landing page](https://www.spinorama.org/docs/images/speaker-box.png)

- **Price**: a reference price in USD per speaker when available. It may differ
  by country, retailer, currency, and date.

- **Preference score**: an aggregate computed from the Spinorama data. Higher
  generally indicates a more preferred response under the model, but the score
  is not a complete measure of quality or maximum output.

  - The score may be marked unavailable for shapes such as surround, in-wall,
    or column speakers where the model is not a good fit. The predicted
    in-room response is a model, not a simulation of your room.
  - Treat small differences cautiously; measurement quality and processing can
    affect the result.
  - Smoothing or incomplete data can improve or worsen a score independently
    of the physical speaker.
  - The score does not describe distortion, compression, maximum output, or
    reliability.
  - The implementation is available in
    [`src/spinorama/compute`](https://github.com/pierreaubert/spinorama/tree/develop/src/spinorama/compute).

- **Bass extension**: the low-frequency extension (LFX) estimates where the
  sound-power response falls below a reference level. Lower frequency is
  generally better, provided output and distortion remain acceptable.

  It is not the same as the frequency of the -3 dB point. It uses the sound
  power response and a reference level derived from the listening window so
  that bass extension is comparable across speakers.

- **Flatness**: the variation in dB around the average on-axis SPL between
  300 Hz and 3 kHz. Lower is better.
